name: Self-contained: no borrowed affect from outside the text
instruction: Score 1.0 when every fact needed to feel the story's emotional payoff is supplied inside the text itself. Score 0.0 when the piece leans on a named franchise, an earlier installment, or unlinked thread/series context to supply the recognition or feeling, so a reader with zero outside knowledge misses the point. Score 0.5 when the story is followable without outside knowledge but one specific beat (a callback, a name, a twist) lands harder only for a reader who already has the context — the story still stands, it just loses one payoff. Exception: if the prompt itself names the borrowed material, using it is licensed; only score against the story if it adds nothing beyond the borrowed reference.

name: Self-contained: no borrowed affect from outside the text
instruction: Test: could a reader who has read only this text (and the prompt) feel the story's intended emotional effect in full? Score 1.0 if yes. Score 0.0 if the effect depends on recognizing an existing franchise, a prior installment in a series, or an off-page continuity the text assumes but does not supply. Score 0.5 if the story mostly works standalone but one specific detail (a name-drop, a reference, a returning character) is clearly aimed at readers with outside context and lands as inert or confusing without it. Do not penalize invented in-story lore the text itself explains; only penalize dependence on knowledge from OUTSIDE this text and prompt.

name: Self-contained: no borrowed affect from outside the text
instruction: Judge self-containment of emotional effect. HIGH (1.0): a first-time reader with no franchise knowledge, no memory of an earlier post, and no link clicked gets the complete emotional arc from this text alone. LOW (0.0): the story's punch depends on already knowing a character, a prior chapter, or a linked continuity — remove that outside knowledge and the ending falls flat or reads as unearned. MID (0.5): the story is emotionally complete on its own but one secondary element (not the core payoff) rewards outside familiarity. If the writing prompt itself supplies the outside material, that material counts as given, not borrowed — only judge whether the story does anything beyond restating it.

name: Embodied nonhuman perspective
instruction: Score 1.0 when the narrator is nonhuman or altered (animal, alien, AI, ghost, hive-mind, etc.) AND its perceptions, values, or metaphors are consistently shaped by that nature throughout — what it notices, what it compares things to, what it takes for granted differs from a human's. Score 0.0 when the narrator is nominally nonhuman but thinks, values, and metaphorizes exactly like a contemporary human — the nonhuman label is decorative. Score 0.5 when the nonhuman framing shapes the narration in places but lapses into generic human interiority elsewhere, or when the nonhuman element is present but thin (one sensory quirk, otherwise human reasoning). If the narrator is human, score 0.0 (the criterion does not apply, and 'no evidence of the trait' is a fail, not NA).

name: Embodied nonhuman perspective
instruction: Ask: does this narrator's nonhuman (or altered-human) nature change HOW it perceives and reasons, not just what label it wears? Score 1.0: the narrator's priorities, sensory emphasis, or comparisons are things a human narrator would not produce (e.g. a dog narrator organizing the world by smell-intensity and pack-status; a hive-mind using 'we' with no singular self-concept). Score 0.0: the narrator could be swapped for a human with no rewrite needed except a noun. Score 0.5: partial — the nonhuman condition surfaces in a few passages (an early establishing beat) but the bulk of the narration reasons like an ordinary human character. A human narrator scores 0.0.

name: Embodied nonhuman perspective
instruction: Look specifically at what the narrator finds notable, urgent, or strange, and what it compares new things to. Score 1.0 if those choices are legibly downstream of a nonhuman condition (a different body, senses, lifespan, or cognition) sustained across the piece. Score 0.5 if this shows up only briefly or inconsistently — human default reasoning takes over for most of the text. Score 0.0 if the narrator's noticing and comparing are indistinguishable from an ordinary contemporary human's, regardless of what species or entity it is labeled as, OR if the narrator is human to begin with.

name: Sustained in-world idiolect in the narration
instruction: Score 1.0 when the narration itself — not just dialogue — is phrased in concepts, terms, or framings that belong to the story's world rather than neutral contemporary English (examples: an alien's log calling whiskey 'a noxious potion'; a bureaucratic containment memo with its own dating convention and euphemisms; a demon narrator that has no word for 'sin' and describes it functionally instead), and this holds through most of the piece. Score 0.5 when the narration has some invented terminology or flavor (proper nouns, one or two coined terms) but otherwise reasons and phrases things in generic modern idiom. Score 0.0 when the narration reads as ordinary contemporary English with only genre nouns swapped in, and the same sentences could belong to any other story unchanged. Credit only invented FRAMES OF REFERENCE (how the narrator conceptualizes things), not just invented names.

name: Sustained in-world idiolect in the narration
instruction: Read the narration voice, separate from dialogue and separate from setting nouns. Does it think in the concepts its world would actually supply — a distinct vocabulary for time, kinship, danger, morality, or technology that a modern human narrator would not reach for? Score 1.0: yes, sustained to near the end. Score 0.5: yes in isolated passages, but the narration reverts to standard modern phrasing for most of the piece. Score 0.0: the narration is indistinguishable from default contemporary prose apart from proper nouns; a reader could lift entire paragraphs into an unrelated story with no rewrite.

name: Sustained in-world idiolect in the narration
instruction: Diagnostic: pick three narration sentences (not dialogue) at random from the piece. Could each be transplanted into a different, unrelated story with zero changes beyond proper nouns? Score 0.0 if yes for all three (generic narration). Score 1.0 if the narrator's own conceptual vocabulary — how it names, measures, or explains things — makes at least two of the three sentences clearly untransplantable, and this pattern holds through most of the story, not just an opening flourish. Score 0.5 for an isolated flourish (one striking early line) without sustained follow-through, or if only one of the three sentences shows the pattern.

name: Story stands alone without external paratext
instruction: Score 1.0 when every fact required to understand and finish the story is contained in the story text itself — no hyperlink, footer note, 'part of my ongoing saga' framing, or subreddit-plug is load-bearing for comprehension. Score 0.0 when the piece explicitly directs the reader elsewhere (a linked prior post, 'see part 4', an out-of-fiction author's note) to supply plot-relevant information or to make the ending land. Score 0.5 when there IS paratext (a footer, a note, a series reference) but it is inessential — the story is fully comprehensible without reading it, the note just adds extra context for fans. A story with no paratext at all and nothing missing scores 1.0, not NA.

name: Story stands alone without external paratext
instruction: Strip away any footer notes, links, or author asides in your mind and ask: is the story complete? Score 1.0 if yes with nothing lost. Score 0.0 if removing that material leaves a plot hole, an unexplained reference, or an ending that doesn't land because setup lives off-page (in a linked earlier chapter, an ongoing continuity the reader is assumed to already follow). Score 0.5 if paratext is present and mildly enriches the piece (e.g., 'part 3 of a series' where each part is independently complete) without being necessary for comprehension. Most stories carry no paratext at all; treat 'nothing to strip' as a clean 1.0, never NA.

name: Story stands alone without external paratext
instruction: Judge dependency, not presence, of paratext. HIGH (1.0): a reader who never clicks a link and never saw a previous post has everything they need. LOW (0.0): comprehension or the ending's payoff requires knowledge the text points to but does not itself contain (an explicit 'continued from', a plug that resolves an otherwise-dangling thread, backstory that only exists in a linked post). MID (0.5): non-essential paratext is present (a note, a series marker) but the story reads as finished without consulting it. No paratext present at all is a clean 1.0.

name: Premise as a Causal Engine
instruction: Identify the prompt's specific unusual premise. Score 1.0 when that exact premise is the reason characters make the choices they make and the reason the central conflict exists — remove the premise and the plot collapses. Score 0.0 when the premise is stated once (often in an opening line) and then the story proceeds as a generic scene that could happen with almost any premise substituted in — the premise decorates rather than drives. Score 0.5 when the premise causes ONE plot beat (an opening complication or the ending twist) but the middle of the story runs on generic conflict unconnected to it.

name: Premise as a Causal Engine
instruction: Test: swap the prompt's unusual premise for a different, unrelated unusual premise. Score 0.0 if the story would barely need to change — the premise was never doing causal work. Score 1.0 if the swap would break the plot: the characters' choices, the conflict, and the ending are all downstream of THIS specific premise. Score 0.5 if the swap would break some scenes (usually the opening or closing beat) but the middle would survive largely intact.

name: Premise as a Causal Engine
instruction: Trace the causal chain from the prompt's unusual premise to the story's climax. Score 1.0 if you can follow an unbroken chain — premise causes situation causes character choice causes conflict causes resolution. Score 0.0 if the chain breaks immediately after the premise is introduced: the story becomes a generic scene (an argument, a reveal, a chase) that isn't actually caused by the premise, just set inside it. Score 0.5 if the chain holds for part of the story (e.g. the premise causes the inciting incident but not the resolution, or vice versa).

name: Self-sufficient: no prior installment, source work or link required
instruction: Score 1.0 when a reader holding only the writing prompt and this text has everything needed to follow every person, relationship, and prior event the story refers to. Score 0.0 when the story requires a named earlier installment, linked post, or specific outside source work to be intelligible — proper nouns, grievances, or relationships arrive already-loaded with no in-text explanation, or the text tells the reader to go read something else first. Score 0.5 when the story borrows a widely-known public character or setting (a famous myth figure, a public-domain character) but supplies enough in-text grounding that a reader unfamiliar with the source can still follow the plot, even if some resonance is lost. Inheriting a PRIVATE cast (the author's own prior story's characters) without introduction is always a 0.0, never a 0.5.

name: Self-sufficient: no prior installment, source work or link required
instruction: Check every named person, relationship, and past event the story references: is each one explained inside this text, or does the text assume the reader already knows it from somewhere else? Score 1.0 if fully self-supplied. Score 0.0 if the story depends on an earlier installment, a linked post, or a specific outside work the reader must already know — especially when this is the author's OWN unlinked prior continuity. Score 0.5 for a widely-known public-domain or famous-character borrowing that still gives the plot-relevant facts in-text, so an unfamiliar reader can follow even without recognizing the reference.

name: Self-sufficient: no prior installment, source work or link required
instruction: Ask whether the story explicitly or implicitly says 'you should already know this from elsewhere.' Score 0.0 if yes — a private prior installment, a linked earlier post, or unexplained pre-loaded grievances/relationships between named characters. Score 1.0 if no — everything the plot needs is established in this text. Score 0.5 only for the specific case of a widely-recognized public character or myth used as raw material, where the piece still supplies the plot mechanics in-text rather than assuming familiarity.

name: Formal/structural risk that serves the content
instruction: Score 1.0 when the story departs from a default linear third/first-person prose scene (using, e.g., a found document, an in-world official register, dialogue-only exchange, verse-like line breaks, epistolary form, or fragmented time) AND that formal choice does real work — it makes an effect possible that plain prose narration would not achieve as well. Score 0.5 when the story attempts a formal departure but the form is decorative or partly undercuts itself (adopted for a paragraph then abandoned, or the form does not actually serve the content it wraps). Score 0.0 when the story uses a straightforward scene-then-ending prose shape with no formal experimentation at all.

name: Formal/structural risk that serves the content
instruction: First check: does the story take ANY risk with its form — an unusual document type, a restrictive register, verse-like breaks, dialogue-only, second person, structural fragmentation? If no, score 0.0. If yes, ask whether the form is load-bearing: does it let the story do something (withhold information, create a rhythm, imply a constrained narrator) that ordinary prose narration would not do as well? Score 1.0 if the form clearly earns its keep. Score 0.5 if the form is present but you cannot tell it is doing more than being unusual — it doesn't hurt the story but it also isn't clearly necessary.

name: Formal/structural risk that serves the content
instruction: Identify the story's structural default: is it a conventional prose scene with a beginning, middle, and end told in ordinary paragraphs? If so, score 0.0 regardless of content quality. If the story instead commits to an unconventional form (found-document framing, official/bureaucratic register, verse lineation, dialogue transcript, structural fragmentation, etc.), evaluate whether that form serves the content — makes the reveal, the voice, or the emotional effect stronger than plain narration would. Score 1.0 if clearly yes, 0.5 if the form is present but its payoff is unclear or inconsistent.

name: Contradictory inner motives
instruction: Score 1.0 when a character holds two motives that genuinely pull against each other AND this conflict shows up in more than one place — in their thoughts, in an action, and in a choice with a real cost. Score 0.0 when every character has exactly one stated attitude toward their situation and acts on it without any internal friction — no character wants two incompatible things at once. Score 0.5 when a character's contradictory motives are mentioned or implied (a stray line of internal conflict) but never surface in an actual consequential choice — the tension is named but not dramatized.

name: Contradictory inner motives
instruction: Look for a character who wants two things that cannot both be true or both be satisfied at once. Score 1.0 if this tension is dramatized — it shapes what the character does, not just what they say they feel, and appears in at least two of {internal thought, behavior, a costly decision}. Score 0.5 if a character voices conflicting feelings once but the story never makes them choose or act on the contradiction. Score 0.0 if no character in the piece has competing motives — everyone's want is single and consistent throughout.

name: Contradictory inner motives
instruction: Find the moment (if any) where a character's action visibly costs them something they also wanted, because they wanted two incompatible things. Score 1.0 if such a moment exists and the setup for it (competing motives shown earlier) is present too. Score 0.5 if competing motives are stated or hinted at but no such costly moment occurs — the contradiction stays abstract. Score 0.0 if no character is written with more than one consistent, uncontested motive across the piece.

name: Adds a proposition the prompt did not supply
instruction: Compare the story's content sentence-by-sentence against the writing prompt's own content. Score 1.0 when the story supplies a complication, causal explanation, twist, or emotional claim that is NOT present or implied in the prompt line itself — the prompt is a starting point the story moves past. Score 0.0 when the story simply restates or dramatizes exactly what the prompt already says and stops there, adding no new proposition, OR ignores the prompt. Score 0.5 when the story adds some new specific detail or texture but the core beat is still just the prompt's own implied payoff, reached and not exceeded. Score the INCREMENT over the prompt only — do not credit writing quality here.

name: Adds a proposition the prompt did not supply
instruction: Ask: if you already knew the prompt, would reading this story tell you anything new — a fact, a cause, a twist, a claim about how the reader should feel — that the prompt line itself didn't already contain or obviously imply? Score 1.0 if yes, clearly. Score 0.0 if the story is a direct dramatization of the prompt's own content and nothing more, or does not engage the prompt at all. Score 0.5 if the story adds minor texture (specific names, a setting detail) without adding a new PROPOSITION — a claim, twist, or causal idea beyond what the prompt already stated.

name: Adds a proposition the prompt did not supply
instruction: Treat the prompt as a one-sentence claim and the story as a response. Score 1.0 if the response argues, complicates, or extends that claim with something new (a cause the prompt didn't name, a twist, an unexpected consequence). Score 0.0 if the response merely restates the claim in narrative form — arriving exactly where the prompt already pointed and stopping — or does not respond to the prompt. Score 0.5 for incremental surface detail without a new claim. Judge only the increment over the prompt's content, independent of prose quality.

name: Prompt-detail payoff
instruction: Locate the writing prompt's single most distinctive, unusual detail. Score 1.0 when that specific detail directly determines a later action, revelation, or the ending — the story could not reach its ending the same way without it. Score 0.0 when the detail is mentioned (often near the start, to establish premise) but never becomes load-bearing again — the story would end identically if the detail were swapped for something generic. Score 0.5 when the detail influences the story's texture or one minor beat but is not what drives the ending or the key revelation.

name: Prompt-detail payoff
instruction: Identify the prompt's defining unusual detail, then check the story's ending and its key turn or revelation: does either one depend specifically on that detail (not just on the general premise)? Score 1.0 if the detail is what makes the ending or turn work. Score 0.0 if the detail is name-checked early and then forgotten — the ending would be unchanged if a different, unrelated detail had been swapped in at the start. Score 0.5 if the detail resurfaces but only in a minor or decorative way, not as the mechanism of the ending or the key turn.

name: Prompt-detail payoff
instruction: Take the prompt's specific unusual detail (not the premise in general — the concrete detail) and ask: does the story's climax or reveal use it as a mechanism, or as set dressing? Score 1.0 if the detail is the mechanism — the ending happens BECAUSE of that detail specifically. Score 0.0 if the detail is only set dressing established early and never returned to at a moment that matters. Score 0.5 if the detail returns but plays a secondary role alongside some other unrelated mechanism driving the ending.
